profile.freedomStatement: Owning my own place and not having to answer to a landlord.

profileSummary.headline: Buffer done, strong surplus, deposit in sight

regions.summary: Your income, spending and surplus are already clear: $7,500 in, $4,500 out, $3,000 spare each month.
regions.why: You earn $7,500 a month and spend $4,500, which leaves a $3,000 surplus and a 40% savings rate — the foundations are already in place. Nothing here needs rebuilding, so this village is a checkpoint rather than a project. Keep it accurate, because every later decision is sized off that $3,000.

regions.summary: Emergency buffer fully funded at $13,500, and no debt to clear.
regions.why: Your 3-month buffer target is $13,500 and your gap is $0 — with $50,000 saved you hold about 11.11 months of expenses. You also carry no debt, so nothing is quietly draining the surplus. You said security first, and that part is genuinely finished.

regions.summary: Decide how the $3,000 monthly surplus and $36,500 spare savings are put to work.
regions.why: With the buffer complete and no debt, the whole $3,000 a month plus $36,500 in spare savings is unallocated — that's the real question in front of you. Your home deposit needs about $2,983 a month to land by January 2029, so the split between deposit and long-term investing is tight and deliberate. This is where your plan is decided, not in any single branch.

regions.summary: Where your second goal — building long-term investments — would live.
regions.why: You want to keep building long-term investments, and at 29 with a moderate risk preference and no debt you have the time horizon that makes this meaningful. It rates a 4 rather than a 5 only because your deposit deadline is 28 months away and needs $2,983 of the $3,000 monthly surplus. Learning the ground here now costs nothing and keeps the option open.

regions.summary: Your $120,000 first-home deposit: $36,500 funded, $83,500 to go, 28 months on the clock.
regions.why: Your freedom statement is about owning your own place, and this is the region that carries it. You have $36,500 of the $120,000 funded and 28 months until January 2029, which needs about $2,983 a month — the projection says you're on track, but only just. That tightness is exactly why it rates a 5.

regions.summary: Income built from something you own rather than only from salary.
regions.why: Nothing in your profile points to a business ambition, and your $7,500 salary plus 40% savings rate is already doing the work. It rates a 2 because a side income could ease the $2,983-a-month deposit squeeze, not because you need one. Worth a look only if the idea genuinely interests you.

regions.summary: A high-volatility corner of the map, best understood before any money is near it.
regions.why: You describe your risk preference as moderate, and the price swings here routinely exceed what a moderate preference is comfortable holding. With a deposit deadline 28 months out, money that can halve in a quarter doesn't fit that timeline. It rates a 2: worth understanding, not worth your deposit.

regions.summary: Your own front door, a growing investment base, and a buffer that never moves.
regions.why: You defined freedom as owning your own place and not answering to a landlord — that's the destination this whole map is pointed at. Getting there means the $120,000 deposit funded, the $13,500 buffer still intact, and long-term investing underway alongside it. Everything before this exists to make that arrival unremarkable.

bridges.requirement: Know your income, expenses and surplus
bridges.relationship: You can only protect a surplus you can see
bridges.why: You already know your $3,000 monthly surplus, so this crossing is open. Knowing the number is what let you size a $13,500 buffer in the first place. Nothing to redo here.

bridges.requirement: Emergency buffer fully funded and debt cleared
bridges.relationship: Growth money is money you won't need back in a hurry
bridges.why: Your emergency gap is $0 and you hold no debt, so this bridge is open. That's what makes the $36,500 in spare savings genuinely spare. You said security first — you've earned the crossing.

bridges.requirement: Decide how the $3,000 surplus is split each month
bridges.relationship: The deposit is funded from the surplus, not from thin air
bridges.why: The deposit needs about $2,983 a month for 28 months, which is nearly your entire surplus. Until you've decided that split, the Property Quarter is a wish rather than a plan. Make the allocation call and this opens immediately.

bridges.requirement: Decide how the $3,000 surplus is split each month
bridges.relationship: Whatever the deposit doesn't claim is what can be invested long term
bridges.why: Your investing goal has no target amount attached, so its funding is whatever survives the deposit allocation. That makes the split decision the gatekeeper. Once you know the leftover, the markets question becomes answerable.

bridges.requirement: Decide how the $3,000 surplus is split each month
bridges.relationship: Starting something usually costs time and some money up front
bridges.why: A venture would draw on the same $3,000 and on hours you currently spend earning $7,500. With the deposit clock at 28 months, you'd want the split settled before adding a third claim. Low relevance for you, but the crossing works the same way.

bridges.requirement: Decide how the $3,000 surplus is split each month
bridges.relationship: Only money with no deadline attached belongs in the most volatile places
bridges.why: Almost all of your surplus is spoken for by a dated $120,000 deposit. Until the split is explicit, you can't tell what, if anything, has no deadline on it. That's the honest gate here.

bridges.requirement: Set the deposit target and know what's left over
bridges.relationship: Money put into long-term investments is money not in your deposit
bridges.why: Your two goals draw from one $3,000 surplus, and the deposit already needs $2,983 of it. Every dollar directed to long-term investing pushes the January 2029 deposit date out. This bridge exists so the trade-off is a choice, not an accident.

bridges.relationship: The deposit is the door to your freedom statement
bridges.why: You said freedom is owning your own place, and $83,500 still stands between you and that. When the deposit is funded and the buffer is untouched, this crossing opens. That is the arrival you described.

bridges.requirement: A long-term investing habit running alongside the deposit
bridges.relationship: Investments keep working after the house is bought
bridges.why: Owning the place ends the landlord problem but not the money question. A long-term investment base is what keeps the freedom durable once the mortgage starts. It's your second goal for good reason.

steps.title: Confirm your monthly numbers
steps.description: Check that $7,500 income and $4,500 expenses still match reality for the coming year.
steps.why: Your whole plan is sized off a $3,000 surplus, so a drift of a few hundred dollars changes the deposit timeline. At an intermediate level this is a five-minute sanity check, not a rebuild. Do it once and move on.

steps.title: Name the $3,000 surplus
steps.description: Treat the $3,000 monthly gap between income and expenses as a deliberate amount with a job, not a leftover.
steps.why: A 40% savings rate is genuinely strong, and unnamed surplus is the easiest kind to lose. Naming it is what turns it into a deposit and an investment base. You've already done the hard part by creating it.

steps.title: Emergency buffer at three months
steps.description: Hold three months of expenses — $13,500 — as money you don't touch for anything planned.
steps.why: Your gap is $0 and your savings cover about 11.11 months of expenses, so this is complete. The point now is protecting it: the buffer sits separately from the $36,500 you're aiming at the deposit. Complete, and worth keeping complete.

steps.title: Confirm you're debt-free
steps.description: Verify there are no balances quietly accruing interest anywhere.
steps.why: Your debt is $0 and your debt-to-income ratio is 0, which is why the entire surplus is available to you. Debt is the one thing that would reorder this whole map. A quick confirmation keeps it that way.

steps.title: Split the $3,000 surplus
steps.description: Decide, in writing, how much of each month's $3,000 goes to the home deposit and how much to long-term investing.
steps.why: Your deposit needs about $2,983 a month to hit $120,000 by January 2029 — that's 99% of your surplus, so the two goals genuinely compete. Deciding the split explicitly is the single highest-value thing on your map right now. You may also want to decide what the $36,500 spare savings does today.

steps.title: Understand the cost of the 28-month window
steps.description: Learn how compounding behaves over short versus long horizons so the deposit-versus-investing trade-off is clear.
steps.why: Money needed in 28 months and money needed in 28 years behave completely differently, and your two goals sit at opposite ends of that. Understanding why makes the split decision much less agonising. It also explains why the deposit money shouldn't be treated like the investment money.

steps.title: Review the split every quarter
steps.description: Re-check the surplus, the deposit progress and the timeline four times a year.
steps.why: You're on track but with almost no margin — $2,983 required out of $3,000 available. A quarterly check catches a slip while it's still a small correction. Ten minutes, four times a year.

steps.title: Learn how pooled and diversified investing works
steps.description: Understand the common structures used for long-term investing and what diversification actually protects against.
steps.why: Your investing goal has no target or date, which makes it a habit rather than a deadline — the structures you use matter more than the timing. At an intermediate level this is about the mechanics and the risks, not the basics. Learning it now costs nothing while the deposit takes priority.

steps.title: Define what long-term investing is for
steps.description: Write down the purpose and time horizon of your investing goal so it can be sized against the deposit.
steps.why: A goal with no target amount and no date can't compete fairly for the surplus, and right now it's funded at $0. Giving it a purpose and a horizon makes the trade-off against $2,983 a month a real comparison. Your moderate risk preference should be part of that written definition.

steps.title: Fund the $120,000 deposit
steps.description: Build the deposit from $36,500 towards $120,000 by January 2029.
steps.why: You have $36,500 funded and $83,500 to go across 28 months, needing about $2,983 each month. The projection says on track, which is true but leaves $17 of monthly slack. This is the number that carries your freedom statement.

steps.title: Decide where deposit money waits
steps.description: Learn what to consider when choosing where a dated deposit sits for the next 28 months.
steps.why: Money with a fixed date 28 months out has different needs from your long-term investing money — it has to still be there when you need it. Understanding that distinction protects the $36,500 you've already built. It also stops the deposit and the investments getting muddled together.

steps.title: Check the January 2029 timeline
steps.description: Compare actual deposit progress against the $2,983 monthly requirement twice a year.
steps.why: With only $17 a month of slack against your $3,000 surplus, one lean month puts the date at risk. Reviewing early means you either adjust the target date or the split, calmly. Being on track and staying on track aren't the same thing.

steps.title: Test whether this interests you at all
steps.description: Spend an hour honestly deciding whether building something of your own is something you want.
steps.why: Nothing in your profile suggests a business ambition, and your salary and 40% savings rate already fund your goals. This step exists so you can close the question rather than leave it vaguely open. If the answer is no, that's a legitimate finish.

steps.title: Understand the volatility before anything else
steps.description: Learn what drives the price swings in digital assets and how large those swings can be.
steps.why: Your risk preference is moderate and your main goal has a hard date 28 months away — that combination sits badly with assets that can move dramatically in weeks. Understanding the mechanics lets you rule it in or out with reasons rather than instinct. No money needs to be involved to complete this step.

steps.title: Revisit what freedom means to you
steps.description: Once a year, check that owning your own place is still the thing you're building towards.
steps.why: You wrote that freedom is owning your own place and not answering to a landlord, and every allocation on this map serves that. Definitions shift between 29 and 32, and the plan should shift with them. An annual check keeps the map honest.

freedomCity.title: 🏡 Freedom City
freedomCity.narrative: You described freedom as "owning my own place and not having to answer to a landlord" — this is that place, reached with a $120,000 deposit funded, a $13,500 buffer untouched, and long-term investments quietly building behind it. Everything on the map is pointed here.

disclaimers: Free Me provides general financial education, not personal financial advice. It doesn't know your full circumstances — consider them, and seek licensed advice for decisions that matter to you.
